{{Nihongo|'''Ōyamazumi Shrine'''|大山祇神社| Ōyamazumi-jinja}}  is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located on the island of [[:en:Ōmishima|Ōmishima]] in the [[Seto Inland Sea]]. Administratively, it is part of the city of {{ill|Imabari, Ehime|en|Imabari, Ehime|qid=Q461020|lt=Imabari, Ehime Prefecture}}. It was the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' shrine of former {{ill|Iyo Province|en|Iyo Province|qid=Q907829|lt=Iyo Province}}.<ref>[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/images/uploads/EOS070712Ab.pdf "Nationwide List of ''Ichinomiya''," p. 2]; retrieved 2012-3-13 and the head shrine of a network more than 10,000 "Ōyamazumi Jinja" and "Mishima Jinja" throughout Japan.</ref> The main festival of the shrine is held annually on the April 22 by the [[Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|Lunar calendar]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}}</ref>

==Enshrined ''kami''==
The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōyamazumi Jinja is:
* {{nihongo|'''[[Ōyamatsumi]]'''|大山積神|}}, a god of mountains, sea, and war in Japanese mythology, and the elder brother of [[Amaterasu]] and [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]]. <ref>{{cite web|url=http://erizabesu.typepad.com/basic_black/oyamazumi.html|title=Oyamazumi Shrine, Treasure in Seto Inland Sea|accessdate=2009-11-30}}</ref>

==History==
Located on the west coast of Ōmishima Island the shrine is situated at the western foot of Mt. Washigatou (436.5 meters), which is considered a {{ill|Sacred mountains|en|Sacred mountains|qid=Q1595289|lt=Sacred mountains}}. The shrine is in a grove of camphor trees, the oldest of which are between 2,600 and 3,000 years old.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.japanvisitor.com/japan-temples-shrines/oyamazumi|title=Oyamazumi Shrine|accessdate=2019-06-04}}</ref> The origins of the shrine are unknown. [[Archaeological excavation]]s have found evidence that the island was a ritual location in the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|qid=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period}}, and unverifiable legends state that the worship of Ōyamatsumi came from [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] on the {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|qid=Q18097|lt=Korea}} and came to Japan from the Japanese domination of {{ill|Mimana|en|Mimana|qid=Q1790223|lt=Mimana}} under {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|qid=Q313119|lt=Emperor Nintoku}}.   Per the ''{{ill|Izumi Province|en|Izumi Province|qid=Q1047117|lt=Izumi-no-kuni}} [[fudoki]]'', the first shrine was established in {{ill|Settsu Province|en|Settsu Province|qid=Q864163|lt=Settsu Province}} and was relocated to Iyo Province by [[:en:Emperor Suiko|Emperor Suiko]] in 594. In 701, the shrine was relocated to its present site, with construction competed in 716 and a dedication ceremony held in 719. The shrine first appears in the historical record in an entry in the [[Shoku Nihongi]] dated 766, and appears regularly in the subsequent national histories of the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (such as the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' and ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''), rising steadily in official Rank. In the 927 ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is listed as a {{nihongo|''Myōjin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. It was also given the title of {{nihongo|''Nihon Sochinju''|日本総鎮守||}} , or "Protector shrine of Japan". The shrine has been supported by successive imperial courts and warlords, especially by members of the [[Taira clan|Taira]] and [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto clans]], who made it a practice to donate swords and armor to the shrine as votive offerings for success and protection in battle. Due to this practice, the shrine has an enormous collection of weaponry, estimated by some to include approximately 40% of Japan's arms and armor designated as either a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|qid=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure}} or an {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|qid=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}}, including eight National Treasures and 76 Important Cultural Properties (as of 2014).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://setouchifinder.com/en/detail/6711|title=Oyamazumi-jinja Shrine – Japan's Most Extensive Samurai Treasury|accessdate=2019-06-04}}</ref>

The [[Honden]] and [[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] of the shrine were destroyed by fire in 1322 and rebuilt in 1427. Both structures are designated as Important Cultural Properties.

The priesthood of the Ōyamazumi Shrine was hereditary to the Ochi clan, who had been the ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of Iyo since the [[Kofun period]].  During the [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]], the shrine gained in popularity as an unnumbered stop on the {{ill|Shikoku Pilgrimage|en|Shikoku Pilgrimage|qid=Q1972399|lt=Shikoku Pilgrimage}}. Following the [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], with the establishment of {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto}} the shrine was classified as a {{nihongo|National shrine,1st Rank|国幣大社|Kokuhei Taisha}}, and was the highest Ranking shrine in the [[Shikoku]] region. <ref name="Shibuya">{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=諸国神社 一宮・二宮・三宮 |date=2015 |publisher=Yamakawa Publishing Company |isbn=978-4634150867}}{{in lang|ja}}</ref><ref name="Irie">{{cite book |last1=Irie |first1=Koichiro |title=諸国一の宮 |date=2018 |publisher=Idō kyōshitsu Publishing |isbn=978-4901398060}}</ref> During the [[:en:Occupied Japan|American occupation of Japan]] following {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}, some 10,000 pieces of weaponry and armor were relocated to the shrine under the pretext of being dedicated as sacred objects from the {{ill|Imperial Japanese Naval Academy|en|Imperial Japanese Naval Academy|qid=Q2238519|lt=Imperial Japanese Naval Academy}} and [[Itsukushima Shrine]] by authorities who feared that they would be confiscated. The [[:en:Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers|GHQ]] authorities were disturbed by the vast number of swords, and ordered the disposal of all items except those which had already been designated as {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|qid=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure}}s. The shrine authorities responded by secretly burying them and later, after the end of the occupation and the establishment of the Japan Self-Defense Forces, they returned the swords to the Japanese government. 

In 1992, the shrine suffered from an arson attack by leftist extremists of the {{ill|Revolutionary Communist League, National Committee|en|Revolutionary Communist League, National Committee|qid=Q2972178|lt=Chūkaku-ha}} who saw the shrine as a symbol of [[:en:Japanese imperialism|Japanese imperialism]].

The shrine is located seven kilometers from the Omishima IC on the {{ill|Nishiseto Expressway|en|Nishiseto Expressway|qid=Q1799184|lt=Nishiseto Expressway}} (Shimanami Kaidō)<ref name="Okada">{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}}</ref>
